modules.doc:
Portal history: the openings a day note actually entered, and the frontmatter
block that carries them.

One record is one fact — a portal opened, and the first text of an entry was
really typed at a particular moment. The record keeps the portal's UTC
instant, the local opening that names its hour and minute, and the actual
local beginning, so the recognition can be recomputed years later without
trusting the machine's clock or its current timezone.

The block is owned whole: the literal `weaver-alignments` key and its indented
sequence of single-line JSON flow mappings. Everything else in the note — the
other properties, their nesting, the closing delimiter, the body — is copied
byte for byte. The format is canonical on write and strict on read: a record
this module cannot read is refused with the reason, never replaced by an empty
history, because a lost alignment cannot be recomputed.

exports.name: ALIGNMENTS_KEY
exports.doc: The one frontmatter property this module owns, and the only key it writes.

exports.name: AlignmentRecord
exports.doc:
One recorded portal beginning.

`portal` is the opening instant in canonical UTC and doubles as the portal's
identity; `opened` is that same instant written with its original numeric
offset, which is what preserves the local hour and minute the echoes are
measured against. `began` is the actual first-input moment at whole-second
precision, and `entry` is the allocated `N` — or null once that entry has
been deleted, because the fact outlives the entry.

exports.name: AlignmentRead
exports.doc: A parsed history, or why the note's history could not be read.

exports.name: AlignmentWrite
exports.doc: The rewritten note, or why nothing was written.

exports.name: formatLocalTimestamp
exports.doc:
Formats an instant as a local timestamp with its numeric offset:
`2026-11-05T22:55:00-08:00`.

The milliseconds are floored away, because a recorded beginning is whole
seconds and rounding up would report a moment the writer had not reached. The
offset is taken for that same instant, so the stamp names exactly the instant
it came from — including both sides of a daylight-saving fold, which differ by
their offset alone.

exports.name: readAlignments
exports.doc:
Reads a note's portal history.

A note without the key, or with the key left blank, has no history yet: that
is the empty list, not an error. Anything else that cannot be read is reported
with the line and the reason, and the caller must refuse to write — an
unreadable history is never replaced by an empty one.

exports.name: mergeAlignment
exports.signature: export function mergeAlignment(source: string, record: AlignmentRecord): AlignmentWrite
exports.doc:
Adds one recorded alignment to a note's history.

The record is validated first and the note's history is read first, so a
malformed record and an unreadable note both refuse rather than overwrite. A
row already identical in portal, beginning and entry is not added twice; two
devices that entered the same portal at different moments both keep their
record, because neither fact is a correction of the other.

exports.name: detachAlignments
exports.signature: export function detachAlignments(source: string, deleted: ReadonlySet<number>): AlignmentWrite
exports.doc:
Detaches deleted entries from the history it belongs to.

Deleting an entry nulls the records of every entry in the deleted subtree, in
the same plan that removes the text, so a reused `N` can never adopt an older
portal. The records themselves are kept: the opening and the moment are
facts about the day, and they are exactly what the history is for. Two records
that both lose their entry stay two records — collapsing them would erase an
event, not tidy it.

modules.doc:
One thought being written outside its note: the facts a capture is made of.

The composer owns a draft for as long as it is being written, so the note
gains nothing until the moment it is settled. That delay is why the beginning
is frozen this early: the day a thought belongs to, and the moment it began,
are facts about the first committed input — not about when a save finally
lands, and not about when a blank form appeared.

A `ThoughtRef` is a reference *back into* a note, and `N` alone is not enough
to hold one: `N` is reused after a deletion, so the evidence that identifies a
thought is its whole recorded shape — its note, its `N`, its branch and depth,
its root, its recorded day and moment, and its own prose. A reference either
matches all of that in the current source or it is stale, and a stale
reference is refused rather than retargeted at whatever now carries the
number. That is the rule that keeps a deletion from adopting a stranger's
branch.

The draft's clock is here too, and it is deliberately not the note's clock: a
composer measures the time spent writing while the writer is in the composer,
pauses when they leave it, and resumes on real input. It never runs inside the
note's own session, and nothing here can start that one.

Pure: no DOM, no `obsidian`, no filesystem, no timers. `now` is always passed
in, so a test can hold the clock still.

exports.name: CaptureBeginning
exports.doc: The first committed input of a thread root, frozen at the instant it arrived.

exports.name: CaptureInvitation
exports.doc:
An opening a root's first committed input qualified for, frozen with it.

It is the occurrence, not the minute: two schedules may offer the same epoch
minute, and each of them is answered through its own identity and the
generation of its activation. A draft carries every invitation it qualified
for, so a coincident second schedule is acknowledged too — but the note gets
one alignment record, because there is one beginning.

exports.name: DraftTarget
exports.doc:
What an open draft would become, once the writer confirms the move.

Choosing a Realm or a parent is a proposal, never an edit: the same draft has
one text, one beginning and one running clock, and moving it must not cost
any of them. Keeping the request as a value is what lets the surface show the
old and the new parent side by side while cancelling stays free.

exports.name: ThoughtRef
exports.doc:
A reference to one written thought, in the note that holds it.

`b`, `d` and `rootN` are the address the reference was taken under: `b` is the
branch id, `d` the dimension, and `rootN` the `N` of the depth-1 entry this
thought sits under (itself, for a root). They are carried so a later read can
tell a moved thought from a merely renumbered one.

exports.name: CaptureRequest
exports.doc: One thought, ready to be written: where it goes and what it says.

exports.name: CaptureResult
exports.doc: The written thought and the root it belongs to, or why nothing was written.

exports.name: CapturePhase
exports.doc: What the composer is doing, as one of five states.

exports.name: DraftClock
exports.doc:
The draft's own stopwatch.

`baselineMs` is what earlier spans of writing accumulated, `resumedAt` when the
current span started (null while paused), and `shownMs` the last whole second
a surface painted — which is the value a save writes, so a late tick can never
file a second the writer did not see.

exports.name: DraftRecord
exports.doc: What a draft is, as it is stored between sessions.

exports.name: CaptureReceipt
exports.doc:
The receipt of one submission, held only until its persistence is confirmed.

It carries the exact source before and after the write, so recovery can tell
"this landed" from "this did not" without appending anything twice, and it is
the only place a whole note is ever copied. It is deleted the moment the answer
is known.

exports.name: wholeSeconds
exports.doc: Whole seconds, never negative and never a fraction a screen cannot show.

exports.name: freshReceiptId
exports.doc: A fresh identity for one receipt, unique for this device's session.

exports.name: captureBeginningAt
exports.doc:
The beginning of a root, from the instant of its first committed input.

One `Date` produces every field, so the day, the moment and the recorded
timestamp can never describe different instants — including on the two sides of
a daylight-saving fold, which differ by their offset alone.

exports.name: idleClock
exports.doc: A draft that has not started counting: nothing banked, nothing running.

exports.name: elapsedOf
exports.signature: export function elapsedOf(clock: DraftClock, now: number): number
exports.doc: The raw milliseconds a draft has accrued, counting the span in progress.

exports.name: shownOf
exports.signature: export function shownOf(clock: DraftClock, now: number): number
exports.doc: The whole second a surface should paint: the last one, while paused.

exports.name: resumeClock
exports.signature: export function resumeClock(clock: DraftClock, at: number): DraftClock
exports.doc:
Counting begins, from what was already banked.

A paused draft resumes from its own stopped second; a fresh one starts at zero.
The shown second is kept so a resume never redraws a smaller number than the
one that was already on screen.

exports.name: pauseClock
exports.doc:
Counting stops and banks the whole second that was on screen.

The painted second is the one a save writes, never a fresh sample taken while
a write is in flight: a surface that painted `00:00:07` and then stalled for
two seconds must file seven, not nine. That is why the clock takes no instant
at all — pausing is a decision about the digits already drawn.

exports.name: commitShown
exports.signature: export function commitShown(clock: DraftClock, ms: number): DraftClock
exports.doc: Records a painted second; a paused draft ignores it, because it is frozen.

exports.name: proseOf
exports.signature: export function proseOf(index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry): string
exports.doc: The prose of an entry, as written: its non-whisper lines, joined.

exports.name: rootEntryOf
exports.signature: export function rootEntryOf(index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry): Entry
exports.doc:
The depth-1 entry a thought sits under.

A root is its own; every descendant walks up `parent` until it reaches one, so
a thought's Thread is always the entry the walk lands on. That walk is what
makes "the Thread includes its descendants" a fact about the note rather than a
convention a surface has to remember.

exports.name: thoughtRefOf
exports.signature: export function thoughtRefOf(index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry, path: string): ThoughtRef
exports.doc: A reference to `entry` as the note holds it right now.

exports.name: resolveThought
exports.signature: export function resolveThought(index: EntryIndex, ref: ThoughtRef): Entry | null
exports.doc:
The entry a reference still truthfully names, or null once it does not.

Every recorded fact has to match: the `N`, the branch and depth, the recorded
day and moment, the prose, and the root it sits under. A deletion can reuse an
`N` and a later edit can change prose; either makes this reference stale for
good, which is what stops a branch from landing under a stranger.

exports.name: excerptOf
exports.signature: export function excerptOf(prose: string, words = 6): string
exports.doc: A short excerpt of prose, for naming a thought in a picker or a label.

exports.name: ThreadNode
exports.doc:
One thought in a Thread, and the thought it hangs under.

`parentN` is the parent's `N` inside the same note, which is what makes the
list a tree a surface can walk without holding an entry index of its own.

exports.name: ThreadView
exports.doc:
One saved Thread as a surface reads it: its root, the path down to the thought
in hand, and every thought in the root's subtree.

A Thread *includes* its descendants, so "view the thread" is the root's own
subtree rather than a second navigation surface: `nodes` is the whole of it in
document preorder, which is the same order the note draws and therefore the
only order a "next thought" can mean.

exports.name: ThreadMove
exports.doc: The direction a structural motion moves the selection.

exports.name: threadViewOf
exports.signature: export function threadViewOf( index: EntryIndex, path: string, target: ThoughtRef | null ): ThreadView | null
exports.doc:
The view of the Thread `target` belongs to, or null when it is stale.

Staleness is decided by {@link resolveThought}: a reference whose entry was
deleted, renumbered or edited no longer describes a thought, and no surface may
draw one from it.

exports.name: moveThreadSelection
exports.signature: export function moveThreadSelection(view: ThreadView, direction: ThreadMove): ThoughtRef | null
exports.doc:
The thought a structural motion selects, or null when it cannot move.

Previous and next are neighbours in the visible Thread; parent and child are
the tree's own edges, with "child" meaning the first direct child. Nothing
wraps around and nothing is written: a motion past an end keeps the selection
where it is, because a jump from the last thought to the first is not what a
writer reaching for `j` meant.

exports.name: branchLabel
exports.doc: The accessible name of a branch action: what it branches from, and from where.

exports.name: openingLabel
exports.doc: The local hour and minute of a recorded opening, `HH:MM`.

modules.doc: Pads a clock component to two digits.

exports.name: pad2
exports.doc: Pads a clock component to two digits.

exports.name: formatClock
exports.doc:
Formats wall-clock time as `HH:MM:SS` using the machine's local timezone.
`toLocaleTimeString` is never used: it can insert non-breaking characters and
follows locale rules.

modules.doc:
Closing the day.

A close is a decision recorded as one mark: `✓ <time>` on its own line, never
an entry. A day carries at most one, so a second close is refused rather than
appended — the first decision stands.

exports.name: CLOSE_MARK
exports.doc: The one shape a close mark has: `✓ HH:MM:SS`, on its own line.

exports.name: CloseScan
exports.doc: What a note says about being closed: the last mark's clock and the line it sits on.

exports.name: parseClose
exports.doc: Every mark in a note, ignoring frontmatter and fenced code.

exports.name: closeLine
exports.doc: The closing mark, on its own line.

exports.name: planCloseDay
exports.signature: export function planCloseDay(source: string, now: Date): InsertPlan | null
exports.doc: The plan that appends the closing mark, or null when it must be refused.

modules.doc:
Colour is a pure function of the dimension number.

Level `d` is a colour that never depends on the vault, a setting, or another
level: `dimensionColor(7)` has the same value before and after a level 7 entry
exists anywhere. That is the whole fix — the old palette re-spread the ramp
whenever the vault found a deeper level, so the colour visibly jumped.

Levels 1–6 are the anchors. Past them the path continues as an OKLCH spiral:
every nine steps the hue lands back on the purple anchor at a lower lightness,
so level 16 is still distinguishable from level 7.

exports.name: ANCHORS
exports.doc: The six anchor colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.

exports.name: srgbToLinear
exports.doc: One sRGB channel to linear light, the first step into OKLab.

exports.name: linearToSrgb
exports.doc: The inverse: linear light back to an sRGB channel.

exports.name: hexToOklab
exports.signature: export function hexToOklab(hex: string): [number, number, number]
exports.doc: Converts `#rrggbb` to OKLab. Inverse of {@link oklabToHex}.

exports.name: oklabToHex
exports.signature: export function oklabToHex(L: number, a: number, b: number): string
exports.doc: Converts OKLab to `#rrggbb`, clamping out-of-gamut channels.

exports.name: dimensionColor
exports.doc: The colour of dimension `d`, memoised. Pure: nothing else is read.

exports.name: dimensionColorVars
exports.doc: The two custom properties a line or marker carries: colour and depth.

modules.doc:
The destinations Weaver may weave into, and the way back from a path.

`main` is the day note the vault already treats as today's — the core Daily
Notes plugin's folder and format when it can be read, and the two fallback
settings when it cannot. It is reserved: it has no row of its own, its
definition keeps resolving through those existing rules, and every other
context is an explicit user-authored one that Daily Notes never overrides.

The filename language is the one the day plane already expands — `YYYY`, `MM`
and `DD`, each appearing once, every other character a literal. Keeping the
language that small is what makes its inverse exist: `contextDayForPath`
matches a whole vault path back to the context and day it names, so a link can
cross between destinations and the daily view can read every configured note
without a second index of what happened. A format outside that language is
refused here, with the reason, rather than half-read later.

The folder is a literal relative path, exactly as the day plane has always
treated it, and may be nested. Tokens live in the filename only.

Pure: no DOM, no `obsidian`, no filesystem.

exports.name: MAIN_CONTEXT_ID
exports.doc: The reserved id of the day note the vault's own Daily Notes settings name.

exports.name: MAIN_CONTEXT_NAME
exports.doc: That context's display name, which no additional context may reuse.

exports.name: WeavingContext
exports.doc: One destination a thought may be woven into.

exports.name: ContextDay
exports.doc: A path recognised as one context's note for one day.

exports.name: ContextError
exports.doc: What one raw definition could not be used for, and where it sits.

exports.name: ContextRow
exports.doc: One usable definition, with the raw row it was read from.

exports.name: ContextRead
exports.doc: The usable definitions, in stored order, and every reason the rest were not.

exports.name: DayTemplate
exports.doc: One day format, read: its literal folder, its tokens, and its whole template.

exports.name: DayToken
exports.doc: The only tokens a filename format may carry.

exports.name: parseDayTemplate
exports.signature: export function parseDayTemplate( folder: string, format: string ):
exports.doc:
Reads a folder and a filename format into a template, or says what is wrong.

Every letter run in the format must be `YYYY`, `MM` or `DD`, and none may
appear twice: a format the inverse cannot read is refused here rather than
accepted and then silently omitted from the daily view.

exports.name: templateNamesADay
exports.doc: True when a template names a whole day, so a path can be read back into one.

exports.name: contextDayForPath
exports.signature: export function contextDayForPath( path: string, contexts: readonly WeavingContext[] ): ContextDay | null
exports.doc:
The context and day a vault path names, or null when none does.

The whole path is matched, never a folder prefix or a basename: two contexts
may share a folder, and only the complete template says which one a file
belongs to. A path that matches a template but carries no real date is not a
day note of that context.

exports.name: contextDayPath
exports.signature: export function contextDayPath(context: WeavingContext, day: string): string
exports.doc: The path a context's note for `day` has, whether or not the file exists.

exports.name: mainContext
exports.doc: The reserved definition, resolved through the day plane's existing options.

exports.name: effectiveContexts
exports.signature: export function effectiveContexts( options: DayNoteOptions, additional: readonly WeavingContext[] ): WeavingContext[]
exports.doc: Main first, then the additional contexts in stored order: the picker's order.

exports.name: contextById
exports.signature: export function contextById( contexts: readonly WeavingContext[], id: string ): WeavingContext | null
exports.doc:
The context with this id, or null.

`main` always resolves, because it is defined by the day plane rather than by
a stored row; an additional context the vault could not read simply is not in
the list, and every caller refuses rather than falling back to another one.

exports.name: freshContextId
exports.doc: The id a freshly added context carries, immutable from the moment it exists.

exports.name: readContexts
exports.signature: export function readContexts(value: unknown, main?: DayNoteOptions): ContextRead
exports.doc:
The usable additional contexts, and every row that is not one.

Nothing unvalidated reaches a resolver. A row is refused, with the reason,
when it is not an object, when its id is missing or reserved, when its name is
empty or already taken (case-insensitively, so a picker is never ambiguous),
when its folder or format cannot be read, or when another context already
writes to the same path template. `main` participates in those last two checks
when `main` options are supplied, so a row cannot quietly shadow the vault's
own day note.

exports.name: contextDraftError
exports.signature: export function contextDraftError(folder: string, format: string): string | null
exports.doc:
The reason a candidate destination cannot be added, or null when it can.

The settings surface asks before writing a row, so a typo is refused with an
explanation beside the field rather than becoming a stored row that every
later resolve has to work around.

exports.name: sourceDayOf
exports.signature: export function sourceDayOf(path: string, contexts: readonly WeavingContext[]): string | null
exports.doc:
The day a source path belongs to when it is a configured day note, or when it
is an older dotted or dashed day note that predates configured destinations.

The second case is deliberate reading support for notes written before
contexts existed: such a note is recognised by its basename alone and is never
a writing destination. Nothing else is a day note.

exports.name: entryDayLinkTarget
exports.signature: export function entryDayLinkTarget( day: string | null, sourcePath: string, contexts: readonly WeavingContext[] ): string | null
exports.doc:
The creation-day link for an entry whose recorded day differs from its note's.

The target is a full vault path in the containing context's own format, so the
link crosses from one destination to another correctly; a note that is not a
configured destination keeps the basename-relative link it has always had. The
recorded day may be earlier or later than the note's — a branch written after
midnight belongs to yesterday's file — and a same-day or undated entry carries
no link at all.

modules.doc:
The day's own numbers, and the frontmatter that carries them.

They are derived from the note, never incremented blind, so a count cannot
disagree with the text above it. They are written only when a value changes,
which is what keeps a `modify` listener from writing on its own write.

exports.name: DayStats
exports.doc: The three readings the frontmatter carries, plus the close they were counted with.

exports.name: countDay
exports.signature: export function countDay(index: EntryIndex, closedAt: string | null): DayStats
exports.doc: Every entry is a travel; depth is the deepest dimension; durations add up.

exports.name: applyDayStats
exports.signature: export function applyDayStats( source: string, stats: DayStats, day: string | null ):
exports.doc:
Merges the stats into the frontmatter block, creating the block when the note
has none. Every other key and every byte outside the frontmatter is preserved.

exports.name: recountDay
exports.signature: export function recountDay(source: string, closedAt: string | null): DayStats
exports.doc: Recomputes a day note's stats from its own text.

modules.doc:
The day's name, and nothing else.

`dayKey` is the frontmatter's `date`; `dayNotePath` is the file the core Daily
Notes plugin opens for a `Date`, and `dayNotePathFor` the same expansion for a
day the caller already holds; `dayKeyFromName` is the way back from a
filename, so a surface can tell a past day from today's without reading the
vault. It takes no `Date`, so reading a note later never changes a label.

This is the pure half of the day plane. Resolving a path to a `TFile`, and
creating the note, touches Obsidian and lives in `entries/day-note.ts` — the
split is what keeps `core` free of an `obsidian` import.

exports.name: DayNoteOptions
exports.doc: The folder and the filename format a day-note path is expanded from.

exports.name: dayKey
exports.doc: `YYYY-MM-DD`, the day key the frontmatter and the calendar use.

exports.name: dayNotePathFor
exports.signature: export function dayNotePathFor(day: string, options: DayNoteOptions): string
exports.doc:
Expands `YYYY`, `MM` and `DD` for a canonical `YYYY-MM-DD` day and joins the
result with the folder.

A destination is resolved from an explicit day, never from a fresh reading of
the clock: the note a thought is filed in is the day the thought began, which
is a fact the caller already holds even when the save happens after midnight.

exports.name: dayNotePath
exports.signature: export function dayNotePath(now: Date, options: DayNoteOptions): string
exports.doc: The same expansion for a `Date`: the day key, then {@link dayNotePathFor}.

exports.name: dayKeyFromName
exports.signature: export function dayKeyFromName(basename: string): string | null
exports.doc: `2026.10.27` or `2026-10-27` becomes `2026-10-27`; anything else is null.

exports.name: dayFrontmatter
exports.doc: The frontmatter a brand-new day note carries, and nothing else.

modules.doc:
The line-level facts every parser in Weaver shares: where each line starts,
where the frontmatter block ends, and which lines are fenced code.

Both the entry parser and the close parser ask exactly these three questions,
so they are answered once, here, and cannot disagree.

exports.name: CodeFence
exports.doc:
The line-level facts every parser in Weaver shares: where each line starts,
where the frontmatter block ends, and which lines are fenced code.

Both the entry parser and the close parser ask exactly these three questions,
so they are answered once, here, and cannot disagree.

exports.name: FenceScan
exports.doc: Every line carrying a fence delimiter, plus the fields it sits inside.

exports.name: lineStartsOf
exports.doc: Absolute start offset of every line in `source`.

exports.name: FrontmatterScan
exports.doc: Where the frontmatter is: none, closed at `end`, or unclosed.

exports.name: scanFrontmatter
exports.signature: export function scanFrontmatter(lines: readonly string[]): FrontmatterScan
exports.doc: Locates the leading frontmatter block, if the document opens with one.

exports.name: scanFences
exports.signature: export function scanFences(lines: readonly string[]): FenceScan
exports.doc: Every fenced code block, and the lines they occupy.

modules.doc:
The clock row of an entry, and the clocks it is written with.

The row is the entry's last line and carries its two clocks: how long it took,
then the moment it was written, with the day it was written on between them
(`+ 00:04:12 2026-11-05 09:14:22`) so an entry keeps its own creation date
even in a note named for another one. One format for both clocks, `HH:MM:SS`, so
a time of day and a duration are the same shape at the same width — which is
what lets them sit at opposite ends of one rail. The algebra behind it — and
the inverse, reading a clock string back — lives in `duration.bend`, where
`LAWS.bend` pins it and `bend PROOF.bend` proves it; `bend/duration.mjs` is
that module compiled, and this file is its typed facade.

The duration comes first because it is the half that moves: settling rewrites
the head of the row and leaves the moment's own characters untouched. On the
frame the duration labels the left corner and the moment the right.

The generated module sits in its own directory on purpose: a `duration.mjs`
beside this file would win the extensionless `./duration` import, and Vite
tries `.mjs` before `.ts`.

What stays here is what Bend cannot see: milliseconds, which are floored into
the whole seconds the algebra counts in — a clock may only show a second that
has happened — and the sigil, which is text.

exports.name: DurationSigil
exports.doc: The three sigils: `-` open and being written, `=` open and paused, `+` settled.

exports.name: formatClock
exports.doc:
Milliseconds as `HH:MM:SS`; hours are unbounded. Whole seconds are floored,
never rounded: a clock may only show a second that has actually happened.

exports.name: formatDurationLine
exports.signature: export function formatDurationLine(sigil: DurationSigil, ms: number): string
exports.doc: The duration half of a clock row, e.g. `+ 00:04:12`.

exports.name: ClockRow
exports.doc:
The parts of a clock row: the duration, the day it was written, then the
moment beside it.

exports.name: parseClockRow
exports.signature: export function parseClockRow(text: string): ClockRow | null
exports.doc:
A clock row: a duration, a day and a moment, and nothing else.

Either clock may be absent — a draft has no settled duration, a hand-written
entry may carry only a moment — so `null` back means the row is prose, not
that a part of it was wrong. A day is only readable beside a moment: a date
on its own would let a surface infer a wall-clock moment the row never
carried, so `+ 00:04:12 2026-11-05` is prose. The duration half's span is
reported so a rewrite of it can leave every other character of the row alone.

Minutes and seconds are 0–59, so `formatClock`'s own output always reads back.
The duration's separator is required, so a prose line that starts with a plus
is prose. The moment follows the duration; the old moment-first row is not a
clock row, which is what makes an unmigrated note fail visibly rather than be
read with its clock as prose.

exports.name: formatClockRow
exports.signature: export function formatClockRow( time: string | null, sigil: DurationSigil, ms: number, day: string | null ): string
exports.doc:
The whole clock row, e.g. `+ 00:04:12 2026-11-05 09:14:22`, or a part alone.

`day` is the entry's own creation day, `YYYY-MM-DD`; a row with no moment
carries no day either, because a date is read only beside a moment.

modules.doc:
The entry: the unit a day note is made of.

An entry is a marker line `{ B.D.N }`, prose, then at most one clock row
`+ 00:04:31 2026-11-05 09:14:22` — how long it took, the day it was written,
then the moment. The written day is the entry's own; a row from before it
existed has no day, and nothing supplies one from the note's name. `B` is the
branch id (a depth-1 entry's position among depth-1 entries, carried
unchanged by everything beneath it), `D` the dimension, `N` the day sequence
(assigned once, only appended). `N` is identity, `B` is address: `N` never
moves, and `B` changes only when a root is deleted, never on insert.

The marker is matched as a **prefix**, so a title written on it becomes the
first prose line instead of breaking the entry. The clock row is the entry's
last line, which is what lets the duration and the moment label the frame's
bottom rail at its two corners. Markers inside frontmatter or a fenced code
block are text.

`proseLines` is trimmed at both ends: a blank line between the prose and the
clock row is spacing, not content, so the caret and the "last prose line" both
refer to a line the writer actually typed on.

A whisper row — `~ <text>`, or `~ learn:` / `~ next:` — is not prose. It is the
model's reading of the entry, written above the writer's words, and it is
partitioned out here so that `title`, `proseFrom` and the duration row all
describe what the writer wrote. A `~` line inside a fenced block is text, and
stays prose.

exports.name: Entry
exports.doc: One entry: its marker, prose, clocks, and the offsets every surface reads.

exports.name: EntryIndex
exports.doc: One parse of a note: its entries, maxima, and the line facts they were found in.

exports.name: MarkerPrefix
exports.doc: What a marker line carries, and how much of the text it occupies.

exports.name: parseMarkerPrefix
exports.signature: export function parseMarkerPrefix(text: string): MarkerPrefix | null
exports.doc:
Reads a marker at the start of `text`, or returns null.

The marker is a prefix, so `{ 1.2.3 } a title` is one entry whose title is
`a title` — and the same is true of a hand-written line that opens with an
address and nothing else.

exports.name: parseEntries
exports.doc: Parses a note into entries, ignoring frontmatter and fenced code.

exports.name: findEntryAtLine
exports.signature: export function findEntryAtLine(index: EntryIndex, line: number): Entry | null
exports.doc: The entry whose block contains this zero-based line, or null.

exports.name: findEntryAtOffset
