exports.name: findCurrentEntry
exports.signature: export function findCurrentEntry(index: EntryIndex, line: number): Entry | null
exports.doc: The entry on `line`, else the nearest one above it, else null.

exports.name: entryBySeq
exports.signature: export function entryBySeq(index: EntryIndex, n: number): Entry | null
exports.doc: The entry carrying this `N`, or null when a write removed it.

exports.name: childrenOf
exports.signature: export function childrenOf(index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry | null): Entry[]
exports.doc: Direct children of `entry`, in document order; roots when it is null.

exports.name: endOfSubtree
exports.signature: export function endOfSubtree(index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry): number
exports.doc: The last line of `entry`'s subtree.

exports.name: nextSeq
exports.doc: The next day sequence: one past the largest, starting at 1.

exports.name: nextBranch
exports.doc: The next branch id: one past the depth-1 entries.

exports.name: formatMarker
exports.signature: export function formatMarker(b: number, d: number, n: number): string
exports.doc: `{ 1.2.3 }`: branch, dimension, sequence; one space inside each brace.

exports.name: repairBranches
exports.doc:
Changes that put every `B` back onto its branch's id.

A root's `B` is its 1-based position among roots, and a deeper entry's `B` is
its root's — so deleting a root is the only thing that can unsettle a branch,
and one pass over the note rewrites exactly the markers that drifted.

modules.doc:
The frame around one entry: a box, and nothing else.

The layer that uses this draws a border and the live highlight. It draws no
text: the entry's own first row — the marker line — is the box's top-left
label, and its own clock row is the bottom edge, labelling the bottom-left
corner with the duration and the bottom-right with the moment. Every label is
read once, from the file, in the place a label would sit. Nothing is hidden
and nothing is duplicated.

Both rails run through the centre of the row that labels them, and the label's
own background cuts the rail behind it, so the box reads as running into its
own text rather than enclosing it. The box therefore spans from one label inset
outside the marker's ink to the right edge of the text column: a box that hugged
its text could not put the duration at one bottom corner and the moment at the
other without a second rendering of the row.

Pure — no DOM, no measurement — so the geometry is testable without a browser.

exports.name: frameLabelInset
exports.doc:
Clearance from label ink to either side rail, matching Reading view's
`calc(0.45em + 16px)`: the label halo must leave the rounded corner visible.

exports.name: FrameColumn
exports.doc: The column a frame may occupy, in the layer's own coordinates.

exports.name: FrameColumnInput
exports.doc: The pane and the content it holds, in one coordinate space.

exports.name: frameColumn
exports.doc:
The column every frame in a view may occupy: from the pane's left edge to one
label inset past the content's right, and never past the pane's own right.

One column serves the drawn boxes and the pending portal tray alike. The
right edge is the content's edge plus one gutter of air, clamped to the pane;
the left edge is the pane's own, because the box below it sits the same gutter
outside the text. A narrow pane is clamped here rather than in each caller, so
a portal can never be narrower than the entries above it.

exports.name: FrameBoxInput
exports.doc: What a box needs: the column, the text's left edge, and the label inset.

exports.name: FrameBox
exports.doc: The rectangle to draw, or `drawn: false` when there is nothing to enclose.

exports.name: frameBox
exports.doc:
The box spans one label inset outside the entry's first row's ink to the
column's right edge.

There is no width below which a box is withheld: a narrow pane gets a narrow
box. The only way to get no box is to have measured nothing yet.

exports.name: ComposerBox
exports.doc: The floating composer's rectangle, in viewport coordinates.

exports.name: ComposerBoxInput
exports.doc: Everything the composer's placement may read.

exports.name: composerHeightShare
exports.doc: How much of a viewport the composer may take, by platform.

exports.name: floatingComposerBox
exports.doc:
Where the floating composer sits.

It floats above the workspace rather than inside a leaf, so it has no flow to
inherit and must be told its box: the writing column of the active pane when
one can be measured, up to 720px centred in the pane when none can, and always
inside the visual viewport with one inset of air. Width is the *text* column —
no widening for the surface and no child indentation — because a thought at
depth 1 is written where the note's own text is.

Height is the surface's own: it sits on the bottom edge and grows upward by
exactly what it rendered, never by a fixed card height it would leave blank.
The cap is the same share of the usable viewport as before, and past it the
surface scrolls inside its own box, so the input and the actions stay reachable
above a phone keyboard. When the usable height is too small to hold a preview
and an input, the preview is dropped rather than letting the box overflow.

A viewport with less room than the insets leave produces a zero-height box at
the floor, never a negative one: geometry that cannot exist is not expressed as
an inverted rectangle.

exports.name: FrameSpanInput
exports.doc: The three rails: this entry's two, and where the next entry's top one sits.

exports.name: FrameSpan
exports.doc: The vertical extent to draw, or `drawn: false` when the rails leave no interior.

exports.name: frameSpan
exports.doc:
The box's vertical extent: from one rail to the other, and nothing more.

The rails are the label lines, so there is no padding to add and no cap to
apply. The old version derived both ends from the text's edges and padded them,
which put the top rail 5 px above the marker's own row and the bottom rail 5 px
below the clock's — so the labels sat inside the box instead of on it, and the
clock row was clipped by the rail under it.

The only judgement left is whether two rails are far enough apart: a box is
withheld when the next entry's rail is closer than {@link FrameSpanInput.air},
because two labels would then share the space and neither would read. There is
no trimming — a rail is a label's centre or it is nothing — and no padding cap.
When the rails cross, there is no interior and no box.

modules.doc:
The plans that write entry text, and the arithmetic every plan shares.

A plan is a list of changes plus the selection to leave behind, applied in one
transaction so a single undo reverts all of it. `+` is never written twice,
`B` is the branch id (inherited on insert, repaired only when a root is
deleted), and `N` is only ever appended.

exports.name: TextChange
exports.doc: One replacement in the document, in absolute offsets.

exports.name: InsertPlan
exports.doc: Changes plus the selection to leave behind, applied in one transaction.

exports.name: planAppendLine
exports.signature: export function planAppendLine(source: string, text: string, caret: number = text.length): InsertPlan
exports.doc:
Appends `text` as the last line, separated from existing content by exactly
one blank line. Trailing blank lines are normalized away, so a note that ends
in three newlines does not collect them above the new block.

A file that ended with a newline still ends with one: the write must not turn
a POSIX text file into a "no newline at end of file" diff.

`caret` is an offset inside `text`; the plan's selection lands there.

exports.name: planChildEntry
exports.signature: export function planChildEntry( _source: string, index: EntryIndex, parent: Entry ): InsertPlan | null
exports.doc:
A child entry one dimension deeper, directly beneath the parent's own block,
above any older siblings: the newest branch is closest to what it descends
from.

The child inherits its parent's written `B`, so a branch carries one branch id
from its root all the way down — and an insert never renumbers anything, which
is what makes it a single change. `N` is still `maxN + 1`, so the new child is
the day's newest entry even when it is shown above older siblings carrying
smaller numbers: `N` is identity, not display order.

The child's clock row is duration-only, like a new root's: `- 00:00:00`. It
gains its own creation day and moment when the first text is typed, from that
input's timestamp, so a child written after midnight under an old parent is
dated the day it was actually written.

exports.name: planEntryBeginning
exports.signature: export function planEntryBeginning( _source: string, index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry, beganAt: Date ): InsertPlan | null
exports.doc:
Stamps a draft's beginning — the day and the moment — into the clock row that
already carries its duration.

A new root or child is written as `- 00:00:00`: a real record with a duration
and no moment, which is exactly what "the writer has not started" means. This
plan turns that row into `- 00:00:00 YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` on the first text,
so both halves describe one input timestamp. The duration half is copied byte
for byte, which preserves a paused `= 00:00:05` as well as an empty `-`.

Nothing else is ever rewritten: an entry that already carries a moment keeps
it, including a historical moment with no day, because a moment is a fact and
not a default. Settled (`+`) entries and entries with no duration are final.
A note this cannot read whole — unclosed frontmatter, an unclosed fence, the
old marker — returns null, as does an `entry` that no longer describes the
current parse. The selection sits in the prose, so a caller can keep the
caret where the text was typed.

exports.name: planCaptureEntry
exports.signature: export function planCaptureEntry( source: string, index: EntryIndex, request: CaptureRequest ): InsertPlan | null
exports.doc:
One settled thought, written exactly as it was written.

Unlike an entry begun in the note, a captured thought is already finished: the
composer held it, timed it and froze its beginning. So the block is written
settled in one transaction — the marker, the prose, and a `+` clock row
carrying the duration and the moment — rather than being created empty and
filled by later writes. Nothing was ever visible in the note before this plan,
so there is no half-written entry for a later step to finish.

A child lands under its parent, one dimension deeper and with the parent's own
branch id, in the parent's file; a root is appended at the tip, with a new
branch id and depth 1. Either way `N` is allocated here and no existing entry
is renumbered.

The planned block is parsed back before anything is returned. A paste can leave
a fence open, or end the prose with a line that reads as a marker or as a clock
row, and either would make the record describe an entry that is not the one
planned here — so the written note must parse into exactly the allocated
entry, at the intended parent and depth, with the exact prose and clock.

An invitation's evidence joins the same plan, and only when it can be truthful:
the thought is a root, an opening was actually announced, and the first
committed input fell inside that opening's own minute. A branch, a draft begun
before the opening, and a draft begun after it closed all carry no record,
because the alignment is a fact about one beginning rather than a reward for
writing. Finishing a qualified draft later changes nothing: the rule is about
when the writing began.

exports.name: planDeleteEntry
exports.signature: export function planDeleteEntry( source: string, index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry ): InsertPlan | null
exports.doc:
Removes an entry and everything under it: the exact inverse of the block
`planChildEntry` writes.

The block runs from the marker to the end of its subtree, the blank separator
lines below it go with it, and every surviving branch whose branch id shifted
is rewritten in the same plan, so one undo restores the whole subtree and the
addressing. The caret lands where the block was.

The deleted subtree's numbers go with it: every alignment record that pointed
at one of them keeps its event — the portal, its opening and the instant the
text began — and loses only the association. `N` is reused after a delete, so
a record left pointing at a number would otherwise describe an unrelated entry
that inherited it. All of it is one plan, so one undo restores the block, the
addressing and the associations together.

exports.name: planDuration
exports.signature: export function planDuration( _source: string, index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry, sigil: DurationSigil, ms: number ): InsertPlan | null
exports.doc:
Writes the duration half of the clock row in place.

A settled entry — a `+` half, or a row that carries no duration at all — is
final: nothing is planned for it, whatever the sigil. An open entry is
rewritten whenever the bytes would change, which the identical-text guard
decides, so a pause that reaches the same second plans nothing. Only the
duration half is rewritten: the moment keeps its own characters, so the row
cannot move, and neither can the day written beside it: everything outside
`durationSpan` is copied byte for byte. The selection is reported at the
prose, because the caller keeps the live selection: rewriting a duration must
not move the caret. A note that
still carries the old marker is refused whole — its old duration line parses
as a clock row, so a field-level rewrite would be the one write that slipped
through the migration.

exports.name: planWhisper
exports.signature: export function planWhisper( _source: string, index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry, whisper: readonly WhisperItem[] ): InsertPlan | null
exports.doc:
Writes a whisper above an entry's first prose line. One insertion, so one
undo.

A whisper is the model's reading of a settled thought, so this plan refuses
every case where it would be a guess: a note it cannot read whole, an answer
with no rows or more than three, an entry that already has one — written once,
never rewritten — an entry with nothing to read, an entry with no clock row to
sit above, and an entry the writer named on the marker row himself. It does
not look at `entry.state`: settle runs while the entry is still `draft`, so
the callers decide who may be whispered.

The inserted text is newline-terminated and the selection lands past it, so
the plan is valid against the text it produces. No caller uses that selection
to move a caret: the writer is somewhere else, by construction.

exports.name: planThread
exports.signature: export function planThread( source: string, index: EntryIndex, entry: Entry, item: WhisperItem ): InsertPlan | null
exports.doc:
Appends one row to an entry that already carries a whisper.

The day pass may add a `thread:` row to a reading written earlier — the day it
refers to did not exist when the reading was written. Nothing is rewritten: the
row goes directly below the last whisper row, so the reading above it is the same
bytes it was.

exports.name: offsetToLineCh
exports.signature: export function offsetToLineCh(source: string, offset: number):
exports.doc: Converts an absolute offset into a zero-based line/ch position.

exports.name: cmChanges
exports.signature: export function cmChanges( changes: readonly TextChange[] ):
exports.doc:
A plan's changes in CodeMirror's own shape.

CodeMirror reads `insert`, not `text`: a `TextChange` handed to a view as-is
is a change with no text, so nothing is written and nothing throws. Every
dispatch of a plan goes through here.

exports.name: applyPlanToSource
exports.signature: export function applyPlanToSource(source: string, plan: InsertPlan):
exports.doc: Applies a plan's changes to a source string; used by tests and previews.

modules.doc:
Where you have been: a real history, with a cursor, not a stack that eats itself.

The old return stack was destructive — walking back popped the place it left,
so going back twice and then forward once was impossible. A history with a
cursor is the ordinary browser shape, and it is the only one that lets a writer
move A → B → C, back to B, forward to C, and back again, without the path
dissolving behind them.

Two kinds of place are remembered. A `NoteStop` is a position inside one note:
the thought it was in, the caret relative to that thought's own prose, and the
scroll offset — captured *before* departure, restored only after the note is on
screen. A `WorkspaceStop` is a whole screen: the layout and each pane's own
state, for a move between destinations rather than between thoughts.

The rule that matters most is the commit rule: a stop is recorded, and the
cursor moved, only after the navigation it belongs to succeeded. A failed jump
changes neither the history nor the screen, so "back" never walks into a place
that was never reached.

Pure: no editor, no DOM, no vault.

exports.name: NoteStop
exports.doc: A position inside one note.

exports.name: WorkspaceStop
exports.doc: A whole screen: a destination's layout and its panes.

exports.name: Stop
exports.doc: One place in the history.

exports.name: NavigationHistory
exports.doc: A history and where in it the writer is.

exports.name: HISTORY_LIMIT
exports.doc: How many places are remembered.

exports.name: initialHistory
exports.doc: The empty history: nothing visited, cursor before the start.

exports.name: record
exports.signature: export function record(history: NavigationHistory, stop: Stop, limit = HISTORY_LIMIT): NavigationHistory
exports.doc:
Records arriving at `stop`.

Arriving somewhere new truncates the forward branch — the future that was
undone is no longer reachable — and the oldest visit falls off past the limit.
Recording the place the cursor already is does not duplicate it, because
"back" through two identical stops would look broken.

exports.name: back
exports.doc:
The previous visit, and the history with the cursor moved onto it.

Nothing is discarded: forward can return to where "back" came from.

exports.name: forward
exports.doc: The next visit forward, and the history with the cursor moved onto it.

exports.name: canGoBack
exports.doc: True when a history can go back.

exports.name: canGoForward
exports.doc: True when a history can go forward again.

exports.name: sameStop
exports.signature: export function sameStop(left: Stop, right: Stop): boolean
exports.doc:
Two stops are the same place.

A note stop is the same when its note, its thought and its caret agree; a
workspace stop when it is the same destination. Comparing the layout itself
would make every unrelated pane resize look like a new place.

modules.doc:
The day's portal history, as rows a surface can list.

What this returns is evidence and nothing else: a note's `weaver-alignments`
record, its original local opening and beginning preserved, and its alignments
recomputed from those frozen facts rather than from the machine's current
timezone. The schedule a record happened to come from is not part of the note,
so it is not invented here — a list of upcoming or pending openings comes from
the live controller, which knows the schedules, and a note's history never
claims that a notice was delivered or that someone declined one.

Nothing here reads or writes the vault. It parses the note it is given and
returns rows, or the reason the note's history could not be read at all.

exports.name: RecordedPortalHistoryRow
exports.doc: A recorded beginning, and the entry it still truthfully points at.

exports.name: PortalHistoryRow
exports.doc: One row in the navigator's portal history: a recorded beginning.

exports.name: PortalHistory
exports.doc: A read history, or why the note's history could not be listed.

exports.name: linkedPortalEntry
exports.signature: export function linkedPortalEntry(record: AlignmentRecord, index: EntryIndex): Entry | null
exports.doc:
Resolves a record's entry only when its clock row still names the recorded
beginning exactly.

`N` alone is not identity: entries are deleted and numbers reused. A record is
trusted for an entry only when the entry still carries the same recorded day
and moment; a manually edited row, a missing entry and a reused number all
resolve to null. Nothing is inferred from proximity or title.

exports.name: portalHistoryRows
exports.doc:
Lists a day note's recorded portal history.

Every recorded event is included, whether or not it still points at an entry: a
record whose entry was deleted keeps its opening and its moment, and loses only
the association. Rows are chronological by opening instant, then by recorded
beginning, and keep source order for otherwise identical events. An unreadable
history is returned as an error and never silently becomes an empty list.

modules.doc:
Invitations: when Weaver may offer to weave, and which offer is outstanding.

A portal is only ever a *time*. Every instant here is an epoch millisecond, so
a daylight-saving gap has no occurrence at all and a repeated hour has two
distinct ones; the frozen local facts a `PortalInstant` carries exist so a
record can say "22:55, at −08:00" long after the machine has travelled.

Two schedule shapes share that arithmetic. The built-in rhythm is the local
minutes the day has always offered — every :00, :11, :22, :33, :44 and :55,
plus each mirrored HH:HH. Configured schedules are explicit: an hourly minute,
selected weekdays at a time, or one instant.

Occurrences are computed from *local calendar days*, not by scanning every
minute since an activation: a schedule enabled a month ago has one outstanding
invitation, not forty thousand candidates. The window a caller asks for is
bounded to the last fifteen local days for weekly schedules (a weekly opening
can be skipped entirely by a daylight-saving gap), the current and previous
local day for hourly ones, and the instant itself for a one-off.

Pure: no DOM, no `obsidian`, no clock of its own.

exports.name: PortalInstant
exports.doc: The local facts of an opening, frozen independently of later timezone changes.

exports.name: AlignmentKind
exports.doc: Exact-second recognitions, never targets or snapped input times.

exports.name: RHYTHM_SCHEDULE_ID
exports.doc: The id the built-in rhythm is stored under; no schedule may reuse it.

exports.name: DEFAULT_LEAD_MINUTES
exports.doc: The lead the rhythm has always had: eleven minutes of notice.

exports.name: PortalWhen
exports.signature: export type PortalWhen = /** Every hour at `minute`, on the device's current local wall clock. */ |
exports.doc: When a configured schedule recurs.

exports.name: PortalSchedule
exports.doc: One configured invitation.

exports.name: PortalSource
exports.doc:
One thing that can offer an invitation: a configured schedule, or the
built-in rhythm.

The rhythm is not a `PortalSchedule` — its minutes are not any single
recurrence shape — so both are described here as a source, and every
computation below takes one. That is what lets one dock list them together.

exports.name: PortalOccurrence
exports.doc: One offering of one schedule: the fact a composer freezes.

exports.name: PortalPhase
exports.doc: A schedule's state now: approaching, open, or gone past its minute.

exports.name: OPENING_WINDOW_MS
exports.doc: How long an opening accepts a beginning: its own minute, and nothing after.

exports.name: PortalScheduleError
exports.doc: One raw stored schedule, and why it could not be used when it could not.

exports.name: PortalScheduleRead
exports.doc: The usable schedules and every reason the rest were not.

exports.name: portalAt
exports.doc: One opening, with the local facts frozen as they were at that instant.

exports.name: occurrencesBetween
exports.signature: export function occurrencesBetween( when: PortalWhen, from: number, to: number ): PortalInstant[]
exports.doc:
Every actual local opening of `when` inside `[from, to]`, earliest first.

The window is walked by local calendar day, so a 23- or 25-hour day costs the
same as any other and a skipped minute simply produces nothing.

exports.name: rhythmOccurrences
exports.signature: export function rhythmOccurrences(from: number, to: number): PortalInstant[]
exports.doc:
The built-in rhythm's openings in `[from, to]`.

It is a schedule like any other: `rhythm:00`, `rhythm:11` and so on, so a day
with no configured schedules still offers the rhythm it always has.

exports.name: portalTime
exports.doc: The local facts of an opening, `HH:MM`, for a label.

exports.name: portalContainsBeginning
exports.signature: export function portalContainsBeginning(portal: PortalInstant, beganAt: number): boolean
exports.doc:
Whether `beganAt` falls inside the opening's own minute.

This is the whole eligibility rule for an entry: writing that *begins* in
`[opensAt, opensAt + 60s)` was written through the opening, and finishing it
afterwards changes nothing. A draft begun before the opening, or after it has
closed, is ordinary writing and gets no record — the rule is about the first
committed input, not about when a writer got around to saving.

exports.name: portalPhase
exports.signature: export function portalPhase(portal: PortalInstant, now: number): PortalPhase
exports.doc:
The phase an opening is in now.

`approaching` is any time before the minute; `available` is the opening's own
minute; `expired` is everything after it. An invitation is not a permission
that waits to be used — a minute that went by unentered is gone, and the next
opening is a different one. Whether an approaching opening is close enough to
show is the schedule's lead, which the controller applies.

exports.name: portalAlignments
exports.signature: export function portalAlignments(portal: PortalInstant, beganAt: number): readonly AlignmentKind[]
exports.doc: Returns every coincident recognition in the opening's original minute.

exports.name: sourceOccurrences
exports.signature: export function sourceOccurrences(source: PortalSource, from: number, to: number): PortalInstant[]
exports.doc: Every opening a source produces in `[from, to]`, earliest first.

exports.name: dueOpening
exports.signature: export function dueOpening( source: PortalSource, now: number, activatedAt: number, acknowledgedThrough: number | null ): PortalInstant | null
exports.doc:
The newest opening of a source that is open right now and this device has not
answered.

The window starts at the later of the source's activation and the last
acknowledgement, so enabling a schedule never replays a month of openings and
answering one opening never hides the next. Occurrences are enumerated over
recent local days rather than every minute since activation, and a candidate
whose minute has already gone by is not due: a missed opening produces no
invitation, no notice and no backfill on wake or restart.

exports.name: nextOpening
exports.signature: export function nextOpening(source: PortalSource, now: number): PortalInstant | null
exports.doc: The next opening at or after `now`, for a source that says when it recurs.

exports.name: scheduleKey
exports.doc: A schedule's identity for a cache that must notice any change to it.

exports.name: readPortalSchedules
exports.doc:
The usable schedules, and every row that is not one.

Nothing unvalidated becomes an invitation. A row is refused, with its reason,
when it has no id, reuses the rhythm's, has no name or destination, or
describes a recurrence the calendar cannot produce.

modules.doc:
The one shape guard for values that arrive as `unknown`.

Settings payloads, vault-local records and stored context rows all cross the
same boundary — data this build did not create — so they all ask the same
question first. One guard, one answer: an object with named fields, never an
array and never null. Fields stay `unknown` until each is checked, which is the
point: this proves a mapping, not its contents.

exports.name: isPlainObject
exports.signature: export function isPlainObject(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown>
exports.doc: True for a plain object: not null, not an array, not a primitive.

modules.doc:
The whisper: the model's reading of one entry, written as `~` rows above its
prose.

A whisper is not part of the record the writer keeps — it is a reading laid on
top of it, and the note has to say so with a character, not with metadata: a
note carries none, so provenance has to survive a reload in the only place a
reader can see it. The glyph `~` is that character. A single leading `~` is
inert in Markdown, and `~~` can never form, because a row needs a space after
the glyph and a row's text may not contain a second one.

Three rows exist, and they divide by grammar, not by semantics: the bare name
interprets the thought, `learn:` names what it has not settled (a noun
phrase), `next:` says what it would do (an imperative). The validator below is
where the writer's register lives — short, lowercase, never negating — so the
rules are enforced on the answer rather than hoped for in the prompt.

Pure: no `obsidian`, and no import from `entries.ts`, so the entry parser can
use this module without a cycle.

exports.name: WhisperType
exports.doc: A whisper row's type: the name is bare, the others carry their word.

exports.name: WhisperItem
exports.doc: One whisper row, parsed.

exports.name: WhisperInput
exports.doc: What a whisper is written about: the entry, and the ancestors it reads after.

exports.name: WHISPER_GLYPH
exports.doc: The one glyph, and the one shape a whisper row has.

exports.name: WHISPER_LINE
exports.doc:
Leading air is tolerated so the editor and Reading view agree: the reading
view classifies on `textContent.trim()`, which has already eaten it. The write
always puts the glyph at column 0.

A type word must be followed by a space, and an untyped row may not open with
one: `~ learn:nospace` names nothing, so it stays prose rather than silently
becoming a name row reading `learn:nospace`.

exports.name: WHISPER_MAX_LINES
exports.doc: Three rows is the ceiling: more is an essay about the entry, not a reading.

exports.name: WHISPER_WORD_LIMITS
exports.doc:
How many words each kind of row may hold.

The name is the anchor — what the navigator shows and what a search would find
— so it stays short. The other rows carry the synthesis, and a reading that
stops at eight words is a label, not a reading.

exports.name: WHISPER_MAX_WORDS
exports.doc: The longest any row may be, so a plan can refuse a paragraph.

exports.name: WHISPER_NEGATION
exports.signature: export const WHISPER_NEGATION = /(,\s*not\b|\bnot just\b[^.]*\bbut\b|\brather than\b|\binstead of\b)/i
exports.doc:
The register a whisper never uses: the antithesis, and only the antithesis.

`X, not Y` and `not just X, but Y` are the constructions the writer rejects. A
bare "not", "no" or "never" is not: dictation says "i need not fear" and "the
data doesn't lie", and a reading that touches those words is describing the
note, not styling it. The earlier rule banned the word as well as the shape,
and rejected a fifth of a real day for saying what the entry said.

exports.name: WHISPER_PROMPT_VERSION
exports.doc: Bumped whenever the prompt's text changes; part of the cache key.

exports.name: parseWhisperLine
exports.signature: export function parseWhisperLine(line: string): WhisperItem | null
exports.doc:
Reads one line as a whisper row, or returns null when it is not one.

The text is trimmed; an empty text is not a row. Anything else — including a
line that merely contains a tilde — is prose.

exports.name: formatWhisperLine
exports.doc: Writes one row back out: the glyph, the type's word when it has one, the text.

exports.name: whisperKey
exports.doc:
The fingerprint of the text a whisper was written against.

FNV-1a over UTF-16 code units, eight lowercase hex digits. It is a
fingerprint, not a security hash: a collision costs at worst one whisper
written against text it did not read, which is the same cost as a stale cache
entry.

The marker, the clock row and every whisper are excluded, so the key answers
exactly one question — *is the text I read still the text that is there?* — and
a write that adds a sibling's whisper, or the sigil changing `-`→`+`, never
invalidates it.

exports.name: validateWhisper
exports.signature: export function validateWhisper( items: readonly unknown[] | null, input: WhisperInput ):
exports.doc:
Checks an answer against the writer's register, in the order the rules are
written in `SYSTEM-DESIGN.md`. The reason is a short literal so a test can
assert on it, and so a failure is one word rather than a sentence.

A validation failure is not a transport failure: the endpoint answered, the
register was not met. `null` means "no answer at all", which is rejected here
as an empty one.

exports.name: WhisperDayEntry
exports.doc: One entry of the day, as the thread question sees it.

exports.name: whisperThreadPrompt
exports.signature: export function whisperThreadPrompt( day: readonly WhisperDayEntry[], own: WhisperDayEntry ):
exports.doc:
The two messages the day-level question is asked with: the day as a skeleton,
then the entry that has to be placed.

The skeleton is one line per entry — an address and a name — never the prose.
The day's full text is four thousand tokens, and a 4B asked to hold both the day
and the entry names the day instead of the entry; a list of names is context it
can actually use.

exports.name: validateThread
exports.signature: export function validateThread( items: readonly unknown[] | null, day: readonly WhisperDayEntry[], own: WhisperDayEntry ):
exports.doc:
Reads the answer to the day-level question.

`null` in the answer is a real answer — the entry stands alone — so the result
distinguishes "nothing to say" from "said something this note cannot carry". A
cited name must exist in the day and must not be the entry's own: a thread that
points at nothing is worse than no thread, because it reads as knowledge.

exports.name: whisperPrompt
exports.doc:
The two messages a completion is asked with.

The ancestors block is only present when there are ancestors: an empty
`ancestors, nearest last:` heading would invite the model to fill it.

exports.name: parseWhisperResponse
exports.signature: export function parseWhisperResponse(text: string): unknown[] | null
exports.doc:
Reads the model's answer: the first `{` to its matching `}` — a naive brace
scan is enough, because the answer is one small object — then `JSON.parse`.

No repair, no retry, no regex extraction of prose: a failed parse is `null`,
which is silently no whisper. A model that wraps its object in a sentence is a
model whose answer is not wanted.

modules.doc:
The `✓` line, banded where it is written.

Like every other decoration Weaver draws, it must come from a **state field**:
a block decoration specified through a plugin throws `RangeError("Block
decorations may not be specified via plugins")`.

exports.name: closeDecorations
exports.doc: The band for every `✓` line in this state, outside the caret.

exports.name: closeDecorationsExtension
exports.doc: Bands every `✓` line outside the caret, in Live Preview only.

modules.doc:
The digit writer shared by every drawn clock.

A clock is three digit spans around two colons; the same spans are rewritten
in place for the life of the element, and no edit ever touches the document.
The ticking itself belongs to `EntryClock`: an element owns no timer.

exports.name: writeClockText
exports.signature: export function writeClockText(digits: readonly HTMLElement[], clock: string): void
exports.doc: Splits an `HH:MM:SS` text into the three digit spans, in place.

exports.name: writeDigits
exports.signature: export function writeDigits(digits: readonly HTMLElement[], ms: number): void
exports.doc: Rewrites the three digit spans — hours, minutes, seconds — in place.

modules.doc: The file a live editor view is showing, or null when it is not a note.

exports.name: editorPathOf
exports.signature: export function editorPathOf(view: EditorView): string | null
exports.doc: The note a live editor is showing, read from the editor's own state.

modules.doc:
The entry, drawn.

Colour and indent ride on two custom properties set per line
(`--weaver-dcolor`, `--weaver-d`), so nothing is generated per level: depth 7
costs exactly what depth 1 costs. The marker keeps its text — only its runs are
marked up, so the line stays editable and the digits stay white while the
punctuation carries the dimension's colour.

The clock row is replaced by a block widget unless the selection touches it;
then it goes back to raw text. Block widgets may not come from a plugin,
which is why everything here is a `StateField`.

Each of those two rows is also a rail's label and carries two extra pieces of
markup: a `weaver-frame-label` mark over the row's own characters, whose
background cuts the rail behind it, and a `data-weaver-n` stamp, which is how
the frame layer finds the row without asking for a DOM position.

The marker row also carries a persistent creation-day link when the recorded
day differs from the day-note filename. Same-day and historical undated
entries need no label. The date is not repeated in the clock widget.

exports.name: entryDecorationSet
exports.signature: export function entryDecorationSet( state: EditorState, session: EntrySession, path: string, clock: EntryClock, contexts: readonly WeavingContext[], openDayLink?: OpenDayLink ):...
exports.doc:
The decoration set for one state. Exported so a test can read it without a
live `EditorView`, which needs a real browser to measure.

exports.name: entryDecorationsExtension
exports.signature: export function entryDecorationsExtension( getSession: () => EntrySession, getPath: () => string, getClock: () => EntryClock, getContexts: () => readonly WeavingContext[], openD...
exports.doc: Publishes the entry decorations as one state field.

modules.doc:
The entry index as editor state: one parse per document change, shared by the
decorations, the keys and the engine, so every surface agrees on structure.

exports.name: refreshEntriesEffect
exports.doc: Forces a reparse, used when a setting or the live session changes.

exports.name: programmaticWrite
exports.doc:
Marks a transaction Weaver wrote itself — a started entry, a submitted one, the
child an advance opens.

The edit listener settles the session on every change the *writer* makes. A
programmatic write must not count as typing: starting an entry would otherwise
start its clock before the first keystroke, and the caret has not even been
moved into the new entry yet when the change lands.

exports.name: InputObservation
exports.doc:
The writer's input, as observed at the moment it happened: which entry it
landed in, and when.

The clock starts on the identity and the time of the input itself, never on
where the caret happens to be when the deferred listener runs — a caret that
moved on in the meantime must not attach the keystroke to another entry, and
the moment recorded must be the moment of typing, not of bookkeeping.

exports.name: capturedInput
exports.doc:
Marks the one transaction that carries an entry's first text together with
its recorded beginning. Its value is the observation, so the listener starts
the clock from the same facts the plan was built from.

exports.name: entryIndexField
exports.doc: The shared parse: one per document change, read by every surface.

exports.name: entryIndexExtension
exports.doc: Registers the field every other editor extension reads.

modules.doc:
The frame around every entry, drawn.

CodeMirror gives each line its own element and offers no way to wrap a range of
lines in a container, so the box is drawn *over* the note: one absolutely
positioned layer inside the scroller, one box per entry, in document
coordinates. The layer draws the border and the live highlight, and no text.

Three consequences, all deliberate:

- **Nothing reflows.** The box catches up to the text; the text never moves to
  fit the box. Every pixel-stability invariant the decorations already keep —
  the clock row's top across a run of insertions — survives.
- **Scrolling is free.** The layer lives inside `.cm-scroller`, which is
  already `position: relative`, so its children scroll with the content and a
  scroll needs no re-measure. Only a reflow does.
- **Editing is untouched.** The layer is `pointer-events: none`.

The file's own rows are the box's rails, and each rail runs through the centre
of the row that labels it: the marker row is the top-left label, the clock row
the bottom edge — its duration at the left corner, its moment at the right —
and each label's own background cuts the rail behind it, so the box reads as
running into the text that names it. Nothing is at `opacity: 0`, nothing is
painted twice, and the frame survives its ends scrolling out of the render
range because a row that is not rendered falls back to the line block's centre.

A different creation day labels the top-right corner. The decoration draws it
— never this layer, which paints no text — and its background cuts the rail.

exports.name: FrameHost
exports.doc: What the layer may ask the plugin: settings, the session, the model, and a fallback path.

exports.name: remeasureFrames
exports.doc:
Re-measures on the next frame, once.

The pending tray is a block widget, so it can be created after the frames
have already measured the note. Mounting it pokes this; nothing per-second
does, because a clock tick is not geometry.

exports.name: entryFrameExtension
exports.doc: Draws one box per entry in a layer inside the scroller.

modules.doc:
The two keys an entry owns, and the two edit events that keep the stopwatch
honest.

`Mod-Shift-Enter` opens the composer from inside any editor as well as from
the app: writing a thought no longer starts an entry in a note, so the chord
belongs to the surface that holds the draft. It replaces the old
`Mod-Shift-E`, which started an entry at the note's tip and revealed it.

`Enter` is two-way and stateless: on an open entry — `-` being written or `=`
paused — it settles the duration to `+` and stops the clock; on a settled
entry it opens a child one dimension deeper under it. `Shift-Enter` is the
newline, on a desk; `Enter` settles everywhere, so a phone's soft keyboard has
no newline gesture and an entry's prose is one paragraph there.

On a phone the clock row is pinned to the bottom of the writing band after
every keystroke, so the stopwatch stays visible above the soft keyboard
without the writer ever scrolling to find it.

exports.name: ENTRY_KEYS
exports.doc:
Every chord an entry claims, for review; `entryKeysExtension` binds each one.

`Mod-Shift-Enter`, not `Mod-Enter`: Obsidian's core "Open link under cursor in
new tab" owns `Mod+Enter` and its scope runs in the document's capture phase,
so neither a `Prec.highest` editor binding nor a command hotkey ever sees that
chord. The shifted chord belongs to no core command.

exports.name: EntryKeyHost
exports.doc: What a key handler may ask for: the session, the edits, and the composer.

exports.name: EntryEditHost
exports.doc:
The same host plus the two edit hooks: `captureInput` decides whether this
input is the first text of an awaiting entry and, when it is, writes the text
and the entry's beginning in one transaction; `captureComposition` finishes
that beginning after an IME commits, or resumes an entry that already has
one; `afterEdit` starts and pauses the clock from the input the editor
observed, not from a later caret.

exports.name: enterableEntry
exports.signature: export function enterableEntry(view: EditorView, _host: EntryKeyHost): Entry | null
exports.doc:
The entry the caret is in.

One rule on every platform: the caret is inside an entry and the view can
write to it. What `Enter` then does depends on the entry's own state, not on
where the caret sits inside it — `Enter` settles an open entry and descends
from a settled one, and `Shift-Enter` remains the newline.

exports.name: handleEnterKey
exports.signature: export function handleEnterKey(view: EditorView, host: EntryKeyHost): boolean
exports.doc: `true` when the key was handled, which stops Obsidian's own binding.

exports.name: handleStartKey
exports.signature: export function handleStartKey(_view: EditorView, host: EntryKeyHost): boolean
exports.doc:
Opens the composer, from inside the editor too.

Always handled: the chord is `Mod-Shift-Enter`, which no other command claims,
so claiming it here cannot take anything away from the writer. Opening it does
not write a byte, and the note the caret is in is untouched.

exports.name: shouldPinStopwatch
exports.doc:
All four must hold: a phone, the live session, the caret on the entry's last
prose line, and a clock row to pin. Each one alone is not enough, which is
what keeps the view still while reading the middle of a long entry.

exports.name: maybePinStopwatch
exports.signature: export function maybePinStopwatch(view: EditorView, host: EntryEditHost, phone = isPhone()): boolean
exports.doc: Pins the stopwatch under the caret on a phone; returns true when it did.

exports.name: entryKeysExtension
exports.doc: Binds `Mod-Shift-Enter` and `Enter` at the highest precedence.

exports.name: inputObservation
exports.signature: export function inputObservation( transactions: readonly Transaction[], context:
exports.doc:
What the writer's input was, read from the transactions themselves.

A capture transaction carries its own observation, so the clock starts from
the same path, entry and timestamp the beginning was written from. Any other
input is observed at the transaction's own selection — never the caret as it
is when the deferred listener finally runs — with the moment of the input.

`null` means this edit was not the writer's text: a `delete`, selection
repair, undo, redo, the vault reloading the note, or a preedit composition
change. None of those may start a clock or be mistaken for a first keystroke.

exports.name: compositionCommit
exports.doc:
The composition commit, as a pair of DOM handlers.

An IME composition's text reaches the document natively — CodeMirror applies
the preedit, and the commit often arrives with no further document change at
all — so the beginning cannot come from the text input handler alone. These
handlers observe the composition's end and finish the beginning afterwards:
metadata only (the text is already the writer's), timestamped at the commit,
named `input.type.compose` so history joins it into the composition's own undo
group. A cancelled composition leaves the document as it was, which is why the
committed text has to still be there before anything is stamped.

Everything the commit is about is captured when the composition *starts*: the
note, the replaced range, and the entry that range belongs to. A deferred
callback then cannot be retargeted by a caret that moved in the meantime —
the committed text must sit exactly where the composition was, in that same
entry, or nothing is stamped. Identical prose elsewhere in the note is not
evidence that this composition committed it.

Exported so a test can drive it without a browser's IME.

exports.name: replacedDocument
exports.signature: export function replacedDocument(transactions: readonly Transaction[]): boolean
exports.doc:
True when this update replaced the document without the writer typing: an
undo, a redo, or a write that carries no input event of its own (a reload, a
rewrite from another surface). A deletion and an in-progress composition are
the writer's own editing, and are not replacements.

exports.name: PendingInput
exports.doc:
What one document update observed, and the generation of the document it was
observed in.

exports.name: InputLedger
exports.doc:
The input observations waiting to be acted on after the update finishes.

A deferred callback runs after the document may have moved on — an undo, a
redo, a reload, another view's write. Those are document replacements without
input, so they end the generation: a captured observation still in flight
cannot start a clock on the text that replaced its own. A later input starts
a new generation with its own timestamp, so typing that follows an undo is
still honored.

exports.name: entryEditExtension
exports.doc: Turns edits and interruptions into session starts and pauses.

modules.doc:
What a drawn frame can be doing, and which single effect shows it.

A box carries at most one effect class at a time, chosen by precedence, so two
states never animate over each other. That is the whole rule: adding an effect
is one entry in `FRAME_EFFECTS` and one block in `styles.css`. Nothing in
`entry-frame.ts` changes, and no surface learns a new name.

Pure and Obsidian-free: the frame layer asks what to show, and the stylesheet
decides what showing it looks like.

exports.name: FrameActivity
exports.doc: The states the frame layer can observe about one entry.

exports.name: FrameEffect
exports.doc: One frame effect: the class it paints, when it applies, and what outranks what.

exports.name: FRAME_EFFECTS
exports.doc:
Every effect a frame can show.

Precedence, highest first, is a statement about transience:

- `is-aligned` (30) is one 800 ms acknowledgment of a captured alignment. The
  recognition is the news; it outranks everything and then yields, because the
  plugin removes the acknowledgment from the activity after it has played.
- `is-whispering` (20) is a request in flight: the model speculating over the
  draft is more transient than the draft itself.
- `is-portal-live` (15) is a captured portal entry being written. It is a
  narrower fact than "an entry is live" — the entry came through a portal, and
  its frame says so with a slow colour pulse rather than the ordinary travel.
- `is-live` (10) is the ordinary running clock, and stays exactly as it was.

A paused portal entry is static: `is-portal-live` requires `live`, so a
captured portal that is not being written carries no animation at all.

exports.name: frameEffect
exports.signature: export function frameEffect(activity: FrameActivity): FrameEffect | null
exports.doc: The one effect a box shows for this activity, or null when nothing is happening.

modules.doc:
The rendered clock row.

The row is the frame's bottom edge, and its two ends are its two labels: the
duration at the left corner, the moment at the right. The widget renders the
row the file holds — the duration from its sigil and milliseconds, then the
moment the parser read — and a half the row does not carry is not drawn: a
moment-only row has no clock at its left corner, and a duration-only row has
no moment at its right. Each half carries its own background, so the rail is cut
twice and stays visible in the gap between them.

Each half is three white digit spans around two dimension-coloured colons — the
same grammar the marker and the date label are drawn in, so the whole frame
reads as one type. The sigil is followed by a real space, exactly as the file
writes it. The day link does not live here: the date labels the top-right
corner and is drawn by the decoration.

Three states decide what the two halves show:

- `fixed` draws exactly what the file holds, and ticks not at all.
- `awaiting` is a draft that has no moment yet: the left corner still reads zero
  and the right corner is the wall clock, because that is the time the first
  input will record. Nothing is written to the note.
- `running` is the live session for this entry: the left corner is the shared
  snapshot's duration, the right corner the moment the text already recorded.

The clock itself belongs to `EntryClock`, not this widget: the widget subscribes
while it is mounted and unsubscribes when it is not. Subscribing paints the last
snapshot without advancing it, so a redraw, a second pane, or an adopted element
never moves the digits and never restarts the elapsed count.

The clock never moves the line. `eq` ignores the elapsed time, so a per
keystroke refresh of the decoration set finds the widget unchanged and leaves
the DOM, and the line's measured height, alone. When something a redraw must
show does change — the sigil, the mode, the colour, the moment — `updateDOM`
rewrites that DOM in place instead of rebuilding it, which is what used to make
the line hop a pixel on every keystroke.

`n` is the entry it belongs to, so the frame layer can find the row by its
stamp instead of by a DOM position.

exports.name: ClockMode
exports.doc: What the row's two halves are showing: the file, a draft's wall clock, a live session.

exports.name: DurationWidgetInput
exports.doc: Everything the widget renders from; none of it changes while the clock ticks.

exports.name: DurationWidget
exports.doc: The clock row as a widget: two labels, digits that tick without a transaction.

modules.doc:
The live editor views, in one place.

A settings change and a rewrite both need the view holding a file; scanning
leaves for it would tie every caller to the workspace's shape.

exports.name: registerEditorView
exports.doc: The registry's only door in, so a test can stand a view in for a real one.

exports.name: unregisterEditorView
exports.doc: Drops a view CodeMirror has destroyed.

exports.name: viewRegistryExtension
exports.doc: Keeps the registry in step with the views CodeMirror creates and drops.

exports.name: registeredEditorViews
exports.doc: Every live view, for a change that must reach all of them.

exports.name: findEditorViewForFile
exports.signature: export function findEditorViewForFile(file: TFile): EditorView | null
exports.doc: The editor showing `file`, preferring the focused one.

exports.name: findActiveEditorView
exports.signature: export function findActiveEditorView(app: App): EditorView | null
exports.doc: The focused editor, else the editor of the active file.

modules.doc:
The one floating draft, and everything that may happen to it.

A composer is not a second editor: it owns no note, holds the bytes of exactly
one unsaved thought, and hands that thought to `EntryEngine.capture` at the
moment the writer settles it. Everything here is about what happens *before*
and *around* that write — freezing a beginning, counting only the time spent
writing, guarding against a second submission, and telling the truth about
whether the note received the text.

Four rules shape it:

 - **One draft.** There is no parking, no slot list and no draft manager. A
   second gesture never replaces the words: it either resumes the draft that is
   already here, or proposes a move of that same draft and waits.
 - **A proposal, not an edit.** Choosing a Realm or another parent is a request.
   While one is displayed the draft keeps its text, its beginning and its
   paused clock; only confirmation revalidates and applies it, and cancelling
   costs nothing because nothing was changed to cancel.
 - **A revision guard.** Every entry point that can change what "this thread"
   means bumps a generation, and an asynchronous answer that belongs to an
   older generation is dropped. That is why a late save cannot reopen a
   composer the writer has already dismissed, and why a stale branch target
   cannot be written under a newer thread.
 - **No invented state.** The draft is written to nothing until `settle`, and
   after `settle` the note is the only authority: the receipt is compared
   against the file's real bytes rather than trusted from local bookkeeping.

The host supplies the world — the clock, the destinations, the one writer, the
workspace visit — so this module touches no note, no vault and no DOM, and a
test can drive every transition with a fake host.

exports.name: CaptureRecord
exports.doc: The whole persisted capture: the draft, and a receipt while one is pending.

exports.name: CaptureStore
exports.doc: Where the one draft lives between sessions.

exports.name: CaptureHost
exports.doc: What the composer needs from the rest of the plugin.

exports.name: SavedThought
exports.doc: A written thought and the Thread root it belongs to.

exports.name: CAPTURE_BUSY
exports.signature: export const CAPTURE_BUSY = "A draft is already open; it was kept."
exports.doc: Why a request to open a second thread was not taken.

exports.name: CaptureController
exports.doc:
The draft, its timing, its destination and its one submission.

Every method is a transition on this object alone; the host is asked only for
the note's text, the one write, and the workspace visit. A method that cannot
proceed leaves the draft exactly as it was and says why through {@link error}.

modules.doc:
The one clock a running stopwatch is read through.

Every surface that draws a ticking clock — the entry's own row, a second pane
showing the same entry, the raw clock row it pauses into — reads this one
instance, so there is one sample per second and one snapshot to stop from. A
widget never owns a timer: it subscribes, paints, and unsubscribes.

A tick samples the real time once, floors the session's elapsed milliseconds to
whole seconds, paints every subscriber synchronously, and only then commits that
painted value to the session. Committing after the paint is what makes
`displayed()` mean "what is on screen" rather than "what the wall clock said".

Subscribing paints the last snapshot without advancing it: adoption, a redraw
or a second view must never move the digits. The timer runs while someone is
painting or while a session is live — an unmounted stopwatch still advances the
shared snapshot, so the next surface shows the right second and a stop uses it.

The tick is scheduled for the nearest of the next wall second and the next
session second, from the actual time each wakeup, so a delayed callback
reconciles itself instead of drifting or replaying skipped seconds.

exports.name: ClockSnapshot
exports.doc: The last instant painted, and the duration that was painted with it.

exports.name: ClockListener
exports.signature: export type ClockListener = (now: number, durationMs: number) => void
exports.doc: Called once per tick with the sampled instant and the painted duration.

exports.name: EntryClock
exports.doc: One sampled, synchronously painted stopwatch shared by every mounted surface.

modules.doc:
Destination travel: going to a workspace, and coming back to it as you left it.

The composer is the reason this exists. Writing somewhere no longer means going
there, so "viewing" has to be its own deliberate act — and if a visit is going
to replace the screen, returning has to be exact: the panes, their files, their
scroll positions and carets, all of it. A destination keeps its *last used*
layout, which is what makes a workspace feel like a place rather than a tab
that reloads.

Four rules keep that honest:

 - The layout is a host object. It is cloned on the way out and never mutated
   on the way in, so no guess about its internal field names is ever made.
 - A failed restore rolls back to the layout that was on screen and *says so*.
   A draft is never lost because a file was missing; if the rollback itself
   fails, the actual screen is labelled "Current workspace" rather than claimed
   to be a destination.
 - The composer's DOM is not a leaf, so a layout change cannot destroy the
   draft's input. Travel freezes the draft's timing and stores it before the
   layout moves.
 - Overlapping travel is refused while one transition is in flight: two

modules.doc:
The day across every destination: one chronology, read and never written.

A day is no longer one note. A thought begun before midnight can land in
yesterday's file while a branch of it is written this morning, and a
destination keeps its own folder entirely. So the day's list is derived from
every *recognised* day note — one whose path a configured destination's
template reads back, or an older dotted or dashed note that predates
destinations — and includes the entries those notes record as created on the
selected day, whatever file they sit in.

The rules that keep the list honest:

 - **Live text first.** An open editor holds the truth about a note it has
   unsaved changes for, so a registered editor's own document is read before
   the file on disk. A list that disagrees with the screen above it is worse
   than a slow one.
 - **No fabricated midnight.** An entry whose clock row carries no moment is
   grouped separately, not placed at `00:00:00`. A missing fact is missing.
 - **Nothing invented, nothing created.** Browsing reads; it never creates a
   note, and an unreadable file is reported with its path instead of quietly
   shortening the list.
 - **Bounded work.** Reads run a few at a time and a newer request cancels the
   generation of an older one, so changing the day twice cannot interleave two
   answers.

Pure of every Obsidian API: paths in, rows out, with the reading injected.

from the exact text the attempt is about to replace, by `writer.ts`, and
skipped when the entry it was aiming at is gone.

return stack before it goes, and carries `programmaticWrite`, so no move starts

modules.doc:
What this device remembers about Weaver, and nothing that syncs.

Two records, deliberately separate. `weaver:local-state:v1` holds the things a
session rebuilds — per-destination layouts, per-pane positions, the last saved
thread of each destination, the active destination, and each schedule's
outstanding invitation. `weaver:capture:v1` holds the one unsaved draft and the
one submission receipt, which must be written together: a keystroke saves a
draft on every commit, and serialising every layout with it would rewrite a
workspace's worth of JSON per character.

Neither belongs in the plugin's `data.json`, which syncs. A draft is the
device's unfinished work, a layout is that device's screen, and an
acknowledgement is that device's answer to an invitation — sharing them would
let one machine's screen rearrange another's, or announce a schedule twice.

Everything here is validated on the way in. A stored value is data that may
have been written by another build, hand-edited, or half-written, so a record
this module cannot read is reported and left exactly as it is: overwriting it
would destroy the only copy of the writer's unsaved words.

cannot be trusted is dropped into `warnings` while the words stay, because a
doubtful record is worth much less than the prose beside it.

modules.doc:
The invitation lifecycle: which schedule is offering what, right now.

A portal stopped being a minute you could write in and became a call to
action. So this controller holds no note, no preparation and no permission:
it derives, from the actual instant, one outstanding invitation per schedule,
and every one of them opens the same composer the writer can open at any time.

Three facts make the derivation honest:

 - **Activation, not history.** A schedule is examined from the moment it was
   enabled, and answered occurrences are excluded, so turning a schedule on
   does not replay a month of openings and a dismissal is not forgotten at the
   next minute.
 - **One per schedule.** A later occurrence replaces its own schedule's
   outstanding invitation; different schedules stay distinct even when they
   point at the same minute. Each invitation carries the generation it belongs
   to, so a late answer can never clear a newer one.
 - **No note bytes.** Dismissing, announcing, or leaving an invitation forever
   writes nothing to the vault. Only a capture that actually settles produces
   evidence, and only through the one writer.

The controller never counts timer callbacks: `reconcile` is called on a
boundary, on a settings change, on visibility, and once after load, and each
call answers as a fresh derivation would.

modules.doc:
The live stopwatch: at most one entry is being written at a time.

The baseline is what the entry's own clock row already holds, so a draft
resumed the next morning continues from where it stopped instead of restarting

Two readings of the same session, and they are not interchangeable. `elapsed`
is the raw sample a clock takes; `displayed` is the last whole second a surface
actually painted. Stopping writes `displayed`, never a fresh sample: what the
writer saw is what the row keeps, so a delayed timer can never make a visible
`00:00:07` become `00:00:09`.

The one writer of a day note.

A note has exactly one writer at a time: the live editor when the file is open
in one, `Vault.process` otherwise — never both. Two writers is what made
Obsidian report the file as modified externally: the day-stats pass landed on
disk behind an editor holding the same note, and the editor's next keystroke
wrote over it (or lost the race the other way round).

The second rule is that a plan is built from the text being written. The
rewrite callback is handed the exact string that will be replaced, inside the
writer, so an append cannot land on a document that moved since it was read.

Weaver: a day note is a linear list of entries, and a thought may be written
from anywhere.

An entry is `{ B.D.N }`, its prose, and one clock row `[+-=] HH:MM:SS YYYY-MM-DD
HH:MM:SS`. Writing happens in two places that share one writer: inside a note,
where the entry is the note's own text, and in the floating composer, which
holds one unsaved thought until it is settled. The navigator is the only list
and the only navigation.

This module is wiring, and only wiring: settings, the one writer, the one clock,
the composer, the invitation dock, the workspace service, commands, and the two
listeners that keep derived facts (day counters, portal association) true.

The model a whisper comes from.

One interface, two implementations: `NoModel` — the default, and what every
test runs — and `OmLxModel`, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

The call goes through `obsidian`'s `requestUrl`, not `fetch`: it is not subject
to the renderer's CORS rules, it needs no `cors_origins` setting on the server,
and a mobile webview cannot block it. It also means an unreachable endpoint
resolves as a failed response rather than a thrown network error, which is the
shape this module already handles.

Why a completion produced no text.

endpoint that never answered are the same silence to the idle speculation, and
completely different sentences to a writer who pressed a command.

treats "no whisper" as ordinary; the runner never asks it anything at all,
since it is the id that turns the whole feature off.

exports.name: OmLxModel
exports.doc:
oMLX's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, one non-streaming completion per call.

`reasoning_content` is never read: a reply that carries reasoning and no
content is empty content, which is this class's whole handling of thinking
models. `max_tokens: 320` is a decision, not a default — three rows of up to
fourteen words plus the JSON envelope need roughly 150 tokens, and the cap is
what stops a model from rambling into a minute-long answer.

modules.doc:
The runner: when a whisper is asked for, and what becomes of the answer.

Two entry points, because the writer's two paths through an entry are
different. `arm` is speculation during a pause in typing: it (re)starts a
short timer, and an answer that arrives before the writer presses `⏎` is
cached, so settle can write it inside its own transaction. `request` is settle
finding the cache cold: it asks at once and lands the answer through the
engine, as its own undoable transaction. Nothing waits on a model.

Failures are counted, not reported. Two transport failures in a row and this
device stops asking until it reloads — a laptop that has left the machine
running oMLX behind should not spend a request per keystroke finding that out.
A *validation* failure does not count: the endpoint answered, the writer's
register was not met.

modules.doc:
Reading view: the same entry the editor draws, in the same frame.

The marker paragraph becomes the frame's first child and the clock paragraph
its last; the prose between them is the frame's interior. The wrapper is a real
element because a box needs one to enclose — and because the file's own text is
what labels it: the marker row is the top rail's label, and the clock row is the
bottom edge, its duration at the left corner and its moment at the right. The
rails run through the middle of those rows and are cut behind them by the
labels' own backgrounds, so the box reads as running into its own text.

The marker's own characters are kept, split into digit runs so the digits stay
white and the punctuation takes the dimension's colour. Anything typed after
the marker stays in the DOM untouched, links and emphasis included. A persistent
top-right link labels a recorded creation day only when it differs from the
day-note filename. Awaiting and historical undated entries carry no date link.
The label never reads the wall clock, and the clock row's two halves stay
time-only: digit and punctuation runs, exactly as in the editor.

modules.doc:
The one bottom surface: a thought being written, and the opening it may count
for.

It is deliberately not a modal, not a leaf and not a widget inside a note. It
floats above the workspace, keeps its draft when the writer travels, and never
moves the note it is writing into. The surface speaks the note's own visual
language on purpose — the same dimension colour, the same rounded frame, the
same rails, the same digit grammar — because a thought written here lands in
that note, and a surface that looked like a different product would make the
writer guess what they were about to produce.

Everything it knows arrives from `CaptureController` (the draft, its timing, its
one submission) and from its host (Realms, saved Threads, workspace travel,
openings). It writes nothing itself: no note byte changes until the controller
settles, and the only thing this file does to the vault is ask.

Five details are load-bearing:

 - **One surface.** The opening's status is a strip inside this card, not a
   second floating card, and the hidden draft is a strip at the same edge.
   There is never a moment where two Weaver surfaces compete for the bottom.
 - **Nothing reflows a note.** The surface is positioned from its own measured
   box, never from padding inserted into a note, so an entry's duration row
   cannot move because a composer appeared.
 - **Focus is never stolen back.** A late save, a re-render or a layout change
   may redraw the surface; only an explicit gesture focuses its input, and Hide
   returns focus to where it came from.
 - **The input is text, all the way down.** Inside it, letters and arrows are
   prose and caret movement. Structural motions belong to the selected saved
   thought, which is its own focusable target.
 - **Committing is one act.** An IME's preedit is never a beginning, a
   composition-confirming Enter is never a save, and a repeated key is never a
   second save.

The one composer.

A single instance serves the app: opening it again is not a second surface but
a second gesture on the same draft, and moving it to another window adopts it
rather than building a twin.

The generated stylesheet: the five numbers a note is drawn with, the two
emphasis colours, and the six anchor colours. Nothing is generated per level —
depth rides on the `--weaver-d` custom property a line carries, so a deeper
entry costs nothing.

The anchor colours are emitted as custom properties for the portal's
multicolour rail, which is the only surface that needs the palette as a
whole. It reads `--weaver-anchor-1` … `--weaver-anchor-6` rather than
restating the hex values in the stylesheet: one palette, one place to change
it.

Writes the stylesheet into a single `<style>` element in `<head>`. Reusing one
element keeps the DOM stable across settings changes.

modules.doc:
The entry-day link at the top right of a frame: `[[YYYY.MM.DD]]`.

The entry's clock row records its day when one was written; a historical
undated row inherits the day-note filename, and the label is written in that
filename's own dotted or dashed style. This generated label names that
recorded day, never the date of viewing. The `weaver-frame-label` background
cuts the top rail behind it. Both surfaces build the same element here, so
Live Preview and Reading view agree.

The element is a span with `role="link"`, not an anchor: the surfaces own the
navigation — `openLinkText` — and an anchor would let Obsidian's own handler
fire a second navigation on top of it.

The link element for `target` (`2026.11.02`), opened from `sourcePath`.

A click or Enter/Space activates it; the event is stopped so the editor does
not also move the caret into the widget. `open` is called with the target and
the note it was clicked from, exactly as `workspace.openLinkText` wants them.

The digit-and-ink grammar: `B.D.N`, the clock row and the date label all split
the same way — digits in the note's own text colour, punctuation in the
dimension's.

Shared by the navigator, the Live Preview frames and the Reading-view frame —
one grammar, every surface. The marker's hyphen is punctuation like every other
separator, because on a framed surface the whole marker is the top rail's label
and its background cuts the rail; there is no character that belongs to the box
instead of the text.

Splits an `HH:MM:SS` clock into digit runs and separator runs inside `parent`:

order, so a ticking clock can write into them.

modules.doc:
How an invitation is named, in the words a writer reads.

Kept out of the dock so the same strings serve the navigator, the notice and
the accessible labels: one invitation, one wording. Every label here is a
function of a frozen occurrence and the current instant, so a countdown can be
repainted without touching any other state.

exports.doc: One invitation as a surface shows it: the occurrence, and how near it is.

exports.name: openingTime

exports.doc:
`Opens in 09:30`, rounded up so a countdown never reads `00:00` before its
opening, or the empty string once it is open.

exports.name: arrivalLabel
exports.signature: export function arrivalLabel(occurrence: PortalOccurrence, contextName?: string): string
exports.doc: `09:11 · Spanish`: when it opens, and the destination it invites writing into.

exports.name: invitationName
exports.doc: The schedule's own name, or a sentence when it has none.

modules.doc:
The navigator: the Realm you are in, the day's thoughts across every Realm, and
the openings that are still live.

It is the only list and the only navigation. Three tabs share one card —
**History**, one chronology for a chosen day; **Realms**, where travelling and
writing are two different buttons because they are two different acts; and
**Portals**, the openings that can still be entered plus the ones that were
really recorded. Nothing here writes an entry: opening a row travels, branching
opens or retargets the composer, and deleting asks the engine after a
confirmation.

Three rules keep it honest:

 - **Browsing is not travelling.** Selecting a row changes nothing outside the
   card; only `Enter`, a tap on the row's own action, or a Realm's `Travel`
   moves the screen.
 - **One selection model.** A stable key identifies the selected row, a roving
   `tabindex` keeps focus on it, and mouse and keyboard update the same value —
   so what is drawn selected, what is focused, and what an action acts on can
   never drift apart.
 - **A countdown is not a rebuild.** A portal tick repaints the text of the rows
   that changed, and rebuilds the list only when the rows themselves are
   different, so the writer's focus survives a ticking second.

It is a self-mounted overlay rather than a `Modal` for one reason: it must never
take a `Scope`. A scope is what once swallowed `⌘,`, and every chord this card
does not claim must reach Obsidian untouched.

exports.name: NavigatorSection
exports.doc: The three things the card can be showing.

exports.name: NavigatorOptions
exports.doc: How the card was opened, so it lands on the reason it was opened.

exports.name: Navigator
exports.doc:
The card.

It owns no note state that outlives a render: every action re-reads what it
acts on, because a write moves every line under it and a stale offset is how a
navigation lands somewhere unintended.

modules.doc:
Which platform this is, as one answer.

Every surface asks here rather than reading Obsidian's flags itself, so a phone
is a phone in the CSS, in the keys and in the pinning alike.

exports.name: isPhone
exports.doc:
Phone detection with the documented fallback: older runtimes may not expose
`Platform.isPhone`, in which case Obsidian's own body class is authoritative.

exports.name: isMobile
exports.doc: True on a phone or a tablet, from Obsidian's own flags.

exports.name: isTablet
exports.doc: True on a tablet, which is neither a phone nor a desktop window.

exports.name: canHover
exports.doc: True when the pointer can hover, so tooltips and hover states are useful.

modules.doc:
The opening, drawn small: one strip, in the same surface as the draft.

A portal is a scheduled opening, not an input and not a second card. This strip
names the opening once — its Realm, its own hour and minute, and what it is
doing — and offers only the gestures that exist: write into it, put it away, or
look at the whole list. It can never accept text, which is the structural reason
a clock cannot be started from it by accident.

It lives inside the composer's own host, so the writer never has two Weaver
surfaces competing for the bottom edge: closed, the strip *is* the surface;
open, it is one line of the draft card's status row. A hidden draft owns the
bottom instead, because resuming it is the more important action.

The rainbow accent belongs to an opening that is live. A minute that has closed
loses it at once and says so neutrally, so colour never claims an opening the
writer can no longer use.

`render` is idempotent and cheap, so a surface may call it on every tick: it
rewrites only the text that changed and keeps focus where it was.
